planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained soil, including rocky or clay sites; established plants tolerate both heat and drought.

directions: Autumn Embers was the original wild-collected selection of seep muhly from north-central Texas, predating and serving as the parent stock from which the more cold-hardy Undaunted was later selected. It forms a dense, finely textured mound of hair-like green foliage that, in late summer, erupts into billowing clouds of pink-tinged inflorescences held on wiry stems well above the leaves. As autumn progresses the pink haze deepens into a warm coppery bronze, giving the cultivar its name, and the color persists as winter interest well after most perennials have faded. Because it lacks the extra cold hardiness later bred into Undaunted, Autumn Embers performs best in the warmer portions of its range. Established plants are extremely heat- and drought-tolerant and rarely bothered by deer or pests.

common_name: Ghana Maiden Grass (Ernst Pagels Red-Plumed Miscanthus)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; deadhead before seed set where Miscanthus sinensis is regulated as invasive.

directions: Bred by the influential German plantsman Ernst Pagels and honored with the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, Ghana forms a dense, upright clump of narrow, bright green blades that reach five to six feet before the flower stems even open. In late summer the plant sends up reddish-brown plumes held well above the foliage on tall wiry stems, gradually fading to silvery white as they mature and persisting for excellent winter interest. Fall color is exceptional even by miscanthus standards, with foliage turning copper, russet, and deep bronze rather than the more common tan of many maiden grass cultivars. Its strongly vertical habit and late bloom time make it a good choice for a back-of-border accent or seasonal privacy screen.

common_name: Gold und Silber Maiden Grass (Gold and Silver Miscanthus)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to fertile soil in full sun to bright shade, with consistent moisture during peak summer heat.

directions: Gold und Silber ('Gold and Silver') is grown for the striking two-stage color change of its plumes, which open in late summer with a warm golden glow as sunlight catches the fine hairs on the newly emerged flower spikes, then shift to cool silvery tones as the season progresses and the seed heads mature. The narrow, arching green foliage forms a dense upright clump reaching five to six feet, providing a sturdy backdrop for the two-toned bloom display. Like most miscanthus, it holds its structure and plume color well into winter before it should be cut back hard in late winter or early spring. It tolerates a range of soils from average to fertile and performs best with consistent moisture during the heat of summer.

common_name: Kleine Silberspinne Maiden Grass (Little Silver Spider Miscanthus)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; its compact size fits mid-border placements where full-size Silberspinne would be too large.

directions: Kleine Silberspinne, German for 'little silver spider', is a more compact sport of the classic Silberspinne selection, staying noticeably shorter and more finely textured than its parent. Slender green blades carry a fine white central stripe that gives the whole clump a silvery cast even before bloom. In summer, thin, spidery, red-brown flower plumes rise in an airy web above the foliage, fading to silver-white as they age and holding their shape through much of winter. Its smaller stature compared to full-size Silberspinne makes it a better fit for mid-border placements or smaller gardens where the larger selection would overwhelm the space.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, leaving ample room for the broad-bladed clump to reach full size.

directions: True to its German name, meaning 'September red', this selection is grown for flower spikes that open in early autumn in a deep brownish-red that is unusually rich for the species, contrasting sharply with the relatively broad, silver-midribbed green blades. It forms a substantial upright clump that can top eight feet in flower, making it one of the larger maiden grass selections suited to screening or as a dramatic focal specimen. The wide leaf blades give the clump a coarser, bolder texture than fine-leaved selections like Gracillimus or Morning Light, and the early, richly colored bloom extends the miscanthus display before most other cultivars begin flowering.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; as a sterile selection it will not reseed, unlike fertile miscanthus.

directions: Silberpfeil, meaning 'silver arrow', is a variegated, sterile selection notable for narrow blades striped in green and silvery white that take on a reddish-purple flush in fall, adding a second season of color beyond the typical tan of most maiden grass foliage. Airy, silvery plumes open late in the season and are prized for cut and dried arrangements as well as garden display. Because it is bred to be sterile, it produces no viable seed, making it a more responsible choice than seed-fertile miscanthus selections in regions where the species has become weedy. Its tall, narrow habit works well as a vertical accent or informal screen at the back of a mixed border.

common_name: Bandwidth Maiden Grass (Compact Banded Sterile Miscanthus)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; its late bloom time and low fertility make it a well-behaved alternative to older banded miscanthus.

directions: Bred at North Carolina State University and released through Darwin Perennials, Bandwidth was developed specifically to solve the reseeding problem that has made some miscanthus selections invasive in parts of the eastern United States. Its green blades carry pronounced horizontal yellow banding, giving an upright, strongly vertical habit similar to Strictus but at roughly half the height, making it easier to fit into smaller gardens. It flowers so late in the season that it essentially never has time to set viable seed before frost, and it also shows improved resistance to rust compared with older selections. The compact, well-behaved habit and reduced fertility make it a good substitute for gardeners who want the classic porcupine-grass banded look without the self-sowing concerns.

common_name: My Fair Maiden Grass (Sterile Bronze-Plumed Miscanthus)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing ample room for its large vase-shaped mature clump.

directions: Another North Carolina State University introduction bred for greatly reduced fertility, My Fair Maiden forms a dense, upright, vase-shaped clump of finely textured green foliage with distinctive pointed white leaf tips. In fall, a profusion of feathery bronze plumes rises well above the leaves and matures to stunning silvery-white seed heads that provide strong winter presence in the garden. Because it sets very little viable seed, it poses far less risk of naturalizing into wild areas than older, fully fertile maiden grass selections, while still delivering the large-scale architectural presence gardeners want from a big miscanthus specimen. The foliage typically turns an attractive tan in autumn before the plant is cut back in late winter.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; a low-fertility alternative to unimproved Gracillimus for gardeners concerned about self-sowing.

directions: Developed by breeders at the University of Georgia, Scout is an infertile, gracillimus-type selection prized for its fine-textured, arching green blades marked with a crisp white midrib. In fall, soft pink plumes rise in a graceful cascade above the mound of foliage and mature to a silvery beige, while the leaves themselves turn shades of yellow, orange, and red for an extended season of color. Because it was specifically bred to be infertile, it does not contribute to the self-seeding that has caused some older miscanthus cultivars to escape cultivation, making it a better-behaved alternative to unimproved Gracillimus for gardeners concerned about spread.

common_name: Sky Rocket Fountain Grass (Variegated Green-and-White Fountain Grass)

planting.note: Plant container divisions after all danger of frost in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; grow as an annual accent or overwinter indoors outside its hardiness range.

directions: Sky Rocket arose as a naturally occurring sport discovered during division of a stock block of Fireworks fountain grass at a Georgia nursery, and it retains its parent's vigor while trading the pink-and-burgundy variegation for crisp vertical bands of green and white. The bold, upright striping gives the clump a bright, almost luminous quality in the landscape or in containers, and the plant sends up soft plumes tinged white to pale purple-pink above the foliage in summer. Like other setaceum selections it is not reliably winter hardy outside the warmest zones, so gardeners in colder climates grow it as a dramatic annual accent or overwinter divisions indoors. It is patented (US PP21,497) and may only be propagated through licensed division, not from seed.

common_name: Red Riding Hood Fountain Grass (Dwarf Purple Fountain Grass)

planting.note: Plant container divisions after all danger of frost in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; its small scale suits containers, edging, and small gardens.

directions: Red Riding Hood is a true dwarf among the purple-leaved setaceum selections, forming a compact vase-shaped clump barely a foot or two tall rather than the three- to five-foot spread typical of standard purple fountain grass. Its plum-purple blades deepen further to dark red in fall, and bottlebrush flower spikes emerge red before aging to tan, giving strong color through most of the growing season on a scale suited to containers, edging, and small gardens where full-size purple fountain grass would be too large. Established plants tolerate heat, humidity, and wind well and can shrug off a light frost, but they are not reliably perennial outside the warmest zones and are typically grown as a warm-season annual or container specimen elsewhere.

common_name: Black Beauty Fountain Grass (Dark Purple-Black Plumed Fountain Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; mulch the crown over winter at the cold edge of its range, as it is slightly less hardy than other alopecuroides selections.

directions: Black Beauty produces the same narrow, arching dark green foliage typical of alopecuroides fountain grasses, but is selected for flower spikes that emerge an especially deep purple-black, rivaling Moudry for the darkest plume color available in the species while forming a somewhat taller, more substantial clump. The bottlebrush-shaped flower heads appear from late summer into autumn and are particularly striking when backlit or rimmed with early frost. It is slightly less cold hardy than many other alopecuroides selections, so gardeners at the cold edge of its range benefit from a protective mulch layer over the crown in winter. Cut the clump back hard before new growth resumes in spring.
